item.title: Trump says Taiwan to buy 30% of Alaska pipeline gas, again predicts lower oil prices
item.description:
Oil’s reaction to Trump’s repeated price forecasts has faded. The market’s own verdict shows in deferred contracts, where WTI and Brent strips for 2027 have recently set records, a sign that traders are pricing a lasting supply squeeze, not a swift resolution. The Alaska deals matter more for gas than oil. Asian buyers locking in North American supply away from the Gulf supports the case for diversification, but the volumes are years away and do nothing for this winter’s tight LNG market. A credible ceasefire would still trigger a sharp drop in crude, so headline risk cuts both ways, but traders are likely to need concrete steps, not statements, before pricing it.

---

Trump brought Asian money to Alaska LNG, but his latest promise of cheaper oil and a swift end to the Iran war meets a market that has heard it before, over, and over, and over again.

Summary:

  • Trump said Taiwan has agreed to buy 30% of the gas from the Alaska LNG pipeline project and invest around $4.4 billion, on top of South Korea’s $50 billion commitment
  • Speaking at a rally in Alaska, he said every permit needed for the project has been granted and that two deals would be announced
  • Trump said oil prices will fall soon and energy prices will drop sharply once the Iran war ends, which he said will happen very soon
  • He said Iran will not possess nuclear weapons and that more oil is being moved out of the Strait of Hormuz than before the war
  • Brent settled near $106 on Tuesday amid escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, and Trump has made similar predictions repeatedly during the conflict

US President Donald Trump said Taiwan has agreed to buy 30% of the gas from the Alaska LNG pipeline project and invest around $4.4 billion in it, as he again predicted that oil prices would fall soon and that the war with Iran would end very soon.

Speaking at a rally in Alaska, Trump said every permit needed for the project has been granted and that two deals would be announced. Taiwan’s commitment adds to the $50 billion South Korea has pledged to invest, giving the long-planned project significant backing from Asian energy importers looking to diversify supply.

Trump also said energy prices would drop sharply as soon as the war ends and that Iran will not be allowed to possess nuclear weapons. He added that more oil is now being moved out of the Strait of Hormuz than before the conflict.

The comments are supportive on their face, but markets may treat them with some caution. Trump has repeatedly said during the conflict that the war would end soon and that oil prices would come down, and so far those forecasts have not materialised. Brent settled near $106 a barrel on Tuesday, while the conflict has widened, with Yemen’s Houthis stepping up missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia and loud explosions reported near Saudi Aramco’s headquarters in Dhahran.

His Hormuz claim is also more upbeat than some outside assessments. Morgan Stanley said recently that Persian Gulf crude exports had recovered to within 10% of prewar levels, a strong rebound but still short of where they were before the war.

The Alaska deals carry longer-term significance. Securing anchor buyers and investment from Taiwan and South Korea strengthens the commercial case for a project intended to send Alaskan gas to Asian markets, reducing their dependence on supply routes through the Gulf. However, a pipeline and export project of this scale would take years to deliver gas, offering no relief to current market tightness.

For oil traders, the test is whether the Iran conflict moves toward a concrete resolution. Until then, the market is likely to keep pricing the risk of further disruption over the promise of a quick end.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Singapore: MAS could tighten again in 2027 if inflation risks materialise, says ANZ
item.description:
ANZ’s view tempers any dovish reading of Wednesday’s surprise hold. If markets come to see it as a pause within a tightening cycle, any Singapore dollar weakness against its trading partners could prove limited. The bar for a further move now appears to be evidence that inflation risks are materialising, which puts imported energy costs at the centre of the outlook. A renewed surge in oil or refined product prices tied to Gulf escalation would be the most likely trigger for MAS to steepen the slope of its policy band again. Easing in crude would strengthen the case for an extended hold.

--

ANZ reads the MAS hold as a breather, not a turning point: the earlier tightenings need time to work, but the door to more remains open.

Summary:

  • ANZ, one of the few forecasters to predict the Monetary Authority of Singapore would hold policy on Wednesday, said MAS could tighten again if inflation risks materialise next year
  • Khoon Goh, ANZ’s head of Asia research, said the effects of MAS’s two tightenings in April and July are still feeding through, so the central bank sees no need to act further for now
  • He noted that third-quarter GDP growth beat expectations and that MAS expects core inflation to stay slightly elevated in the near term
  • Goh said the hold does not mean the tightening cycle is over

The Monetary Authority of Singapore could resume tightening next year if upside risks to inflation materialise, according to ANZ, one of the few forecasters that correctly predicted the central bank would leave policy unchanged on Wednesday.

Khoon Goh, head of Asia research at ANZ, said MAS judged there was no need to tighten further at this stage because the effects of its two earlier tightening moves, in April and July, are still feeding through the economy. Monetary policy works with a lag, and changes to the path of the Singapore dollar take time to show up in import prices and, in turn, consumer inflation.

That was despite a stronger economic backdrop than expected. Goh noted that third-quarter GDP growth beat expectations and that MAS still expects core inflation to remain slightly elevated in the near term. He stressed, however, that the decision does not signal the end of the tightening cycle, and that MAS could tighten again if upside inflation risks emerge next year.

ANZ’s call set it apart from the consensus. All 10 analysts polled by Reuters ahead of the decision had expected a tightening, making [Wednesday’s hold] a surprise to most of the market.

MAS, which manages policy through the Singapore dollar’s trade-weighted exchange rate, kept the rate of appreciation, width and centre of its policy band unchanged. Because the band remains on an appreciating path, the decision leaves the existing tightening stance in place without adding to it. [Our explainer on how MAS policy works] sets out how the three levers operate.

In its statement, the central bank said the economy should expand at a firm pace in the coming quarters before moderating as the AI cycle eases and global financial conditions tighten. It forecast core inflation to average 1.5% to 2.0% in 2026 and to ease more discernibly from mid-2027, but said risks to inflation remain tilted to the upside, including from a sharp and sustained rise in energy or food prices.

ANZ’s assessment suggests the next move, if any, is more likely to be a tightening than an easing. The path of imported costs, particularly energy, and whether core inflation proves stickier than MAS expects will shape the outlook for its upcoming reviews.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: How Singapore’s monetary policy works: the S$NEER band explained in three levers
item.description:
How Singapore’s monetary policy works: the S$NEER band explained in three levers

Most central banks fight inflation by raising or cutting interest rates. Singapore does it differently. The Monetary Authority of Singapore steers the economy by managing the value of the Singapore dollar against a basket of its trading partners’ currencies. When MAS “tightens,” it lets the currency strengthen faster, which makes imports cheaper and cools inflation. When it “eases,” it slows or reverses that appreciation.

That is why Wednesday’s decision to hold policy steady was framed entirely in terms of an exchange rate band, with no mention of an interest rate.

Why Singapore uses the exchange rate

Singapore is one of the most open economies in the world. It imports most of what it consumes, from food and fuel to raw materials, and trade flows are large relative to the size of its economy. That makes the exchange rate a far more powerful influence on prices than domestic interest rates.

There is also a practical constraint. Singapore allows capital to move freely in and out of the country. A central bank with open capital flows can control either its exchange rate or its interest rates, but not both. MAS chose the exchange rate in 1981, and local interest rates largely follow global rates, particularly those in the US.

What is the S$NEER?

The S$NEER, or Singapore dollar nominal effective exchange rate, measures the Singapore dollar against a weighted basket of the currencies of Singapore's main trading partners. MAS does not publish the basket's composition or weights. It manages the S$NEER within a policy band, stepping into the currency market when needed to keep it there.

The three levers

MAS adjusts policy through three features of the band, none of which it discloses precisely.

  • Slope: the speed of appreciation. The band is set on a gradual path, usually an upward one. A steeper slope means the Singapore dollar is allowed to strengthen faster, which is a tightening. A flatter slope is an easing. On Wednesday, MAS kept the slope unchanged.
  • Centre: the starting level. MAS can shift the midpoint of the band up or down in one step, known as re-centring. Moving the centre higher delivers an immediate, one-off strengthening, a stronger tightening signal than steepening the slope. MAS left the centre unchanged on Wednesday.
  • Width: how much movement is tolerated. A wider band gives the currency more room to fluctuate, usually used in periods of market volatility. A narrower band signals tighter control. The width was also unchanged.

Analysts estimate the band’s width and slope from the currency’s movements, but MAS keeps the exact parameters private. That gives it room to act without inviting speculation against fixed levels.

How often MAS decides

MAS reviews policy four times a year, in January, April, July and October, having moved from a twice-yearly schedule in 2024. Decisions are released early in the Singapore morning, which is around midnight GMT.

The inflation measure that matters

MAS focuses on core inflation, which excludes accommodation and private transport costs. Those categories are heavily influenced by government policy and housing and car-ownership cycles, so stripping them out gives a cleaner read on underlying price pressures. On Wednesday, MAS forecast core inflation to average 1.5% to 2.0% for 2026 and to ease more discernibly from mid-2027.

What Wednesday’s decision means

By leaving all three levers unchanged, MAS kept the Singapore dollar on its existing appreciating path. That is still a restraint on imported inflation, just not an increased one. All 10 analysts polled by Reuters had expected a tightening, most likely through a steeper slope, so the hold was a dovish surprise relative to expectations, even though the policy setting itself remains a tightening bias.

Key takeaway for traders

When reading an MAS statement, watch for the words “slope,” “width” and “centre.” Any change to them is the policy decision. For the Singapore dollar, the slope sets the medium-term direction against the basket, while a re-centring can produce a sharp immediate move. Because Singapore’s inflation is so sensitive to import costs, especially energy, oil prices are often a better guide to the next MAS move than local interest rates.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6922 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
Still to come from China:

  • Economic and event calendar in Asia Wednesday, October 14, 2026 - China inflation data

---

The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. 

  • Goldman Sachs says yuan undervalued by up to 25% and markets underestimate how far it can rise
China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Saylor sees Bitcoin above $100,000, says investors will seek (scarce) assets that robots can’t make
item.description:
Friday’s upcoming MSCI decision on whether to exclude companies like Strategy from its global indices is the nearest catalyst, since an exclusion could trigger passive selling of the shares even if Saylor plays down its importance. Strategy’s new willingness to sell Bitcoin as well as buy it removes the assumption that the largest corporate holder is a one-way buyer, adding a potential source of supply in weaker markets. On the positive side, regulatory guidance from US agencies has eased a key overhang. Bitcoin still has to compete for capital with AI stocks and with Treasury yields that have risen sharply this year, so a turn lower in yields after US inflation data would be the clearest macro tailwind for his $100,000 call.

---

Saylor is talking his book, but his core pitch, that AI makes scarcity more valuable, is an argument worth weighing on its merits.

Summary:

  • Strategy executive chairman Michael Saylor said Bitcoin should move back above $100,000 after bottoming slightly below $60,000, with prices now in the $80,000s, but gave no timeframe
  • He argued AI will erode the value of labour-based equities and push investors towards scarce assets such as gold, prime real estate and Bitcoin
  • Saylor cited favourable US regulatory guidance, accelerating bank adoption and tokenisation as new tailwinds, calling the stalling of the Clarity Act good for the industry
  • He defended Strategy’s recent Bitcoin sales as part of running a structured finance company, but said the firm expects to keep adding to its holdings
  • Saylor called MSCI’s possible exclusion of Strategy from its indices, due to be decided on Friday, a bad precedent but said it was not that important to the company

Strategy co-founder and executive chairman Michael Saylor said Bitcoin is entering a new bull market and should climb back above $100,000, arguing that artificial intelligence will push investors towards assets whose supply cannot be expanded.

Speaking to Bloomberg Television at DC Fintech Week on Tuesday, Saylor said Bitcoin bottomed slightly below $60,000 during the past year’s contraction and has since rebounded into the $80,000s. He declined to give a timeframe for his $100,000 target, saying he plans in centuries, not months. Strategy’s longer-term forecast is for Bitcoin to grow 20% to 30% a year over the next two decades.

At the heart of his case is scarcity. Saylor argued that AI will reduce the value of companies built on large human workforces or on chasing the next breakthrough product, while increasing demand for scarce capital such as Palm Beach real estate, gold and Bitcoin. In his words, investors will look for things robots cannot make more of.

The argument has some logic. If AI makes labour and software abundant, assets with fixed supply could gain relative appeal. But it comes from the executive chairman of the world’s largest corporate Bitcoin holder, with a stake he put at more than $70 billion. Bloomberg’s interviewers also challenged it, noting that AI is absorbing much of the market’s capital and that the scarcity rotation has yet to show clearly in Bitcoin, which remains about 30% below last year’s record high.

Saylor countered that since Strategy began buying in August 2020, Bitcoin has returned about 38% a year and the company’s shares more than 50% a year, outpacing gold and every Magnificent Seven stock except Nvidia. By his own description, Bitcoin is also a volatile asset, with volatility of around 40, while Strategy’s shares run at roughly 80.

He pointed to new tailwinds: favourable US regulation, faster bank adoption, the spread of tokenised securities and the growth of digital credit. He said the Senate’s failure to advance the Clarity Act was the best outcome for the industry, as guidance from the Treasury, the SEC and the CFTC proved more supportive than the bill’s restrictions.

Saylor also defended Strategy’s sale of a small amount of Bitcoin in June, when prices were around $73,000, a move that unsettled the market. He described the company as a structured finance business that must be able to buy or sell Bitcoin, equity or credit as conditions require, mainly to support dividends on its credit products. He said those products pay 10% to 12% treated as a return of capital, which defers tax, and that the company expects to keep increasing its Bitcoin holdings in a bull market.

MSCI is due to decide on Friday whether to exclude companies like Strategy from its global indices on the grounds they mainly accumulate assets. Saylor called the proposal a bad precedent, argued Strategy is an operating company like banks and insurers, and said the decision was not that important to the firm. 

Explainer: MSCI, Strategy and the index question

What is MSCI? MSCI is one of the world’s largest index providers. Its benchmarks, such as the MSCI World and MSCI USA, are tracked by trillions of dollars in pension funds, ETFs and other investment products. When a company joins or leaves an MSCI index, funds that track it generally have to buy or sell the shares, whatever their view of the company.

What is Strategy? Strategy, formerly MicroStrategy and listed under the ticker MSTR, started as an enterprise software company. Since August 2020 it has focused on buying and holding Bitcoin, funded largely by issuing shares, debt and preferred-style securities. It is now the largest corporate holder of Bitcoin, with holdings Saylor puts at more than $70 billion.

What are “digital credit” products? These are Strategy’s income-paying securities, such as STRC, backed by the company’s Bitcoin holdings. Saylor says they pay 10% to 12% a year, treated as a return of capital, which generally defers tax rather than removing it. The company may sell Bitcoin or other assets to fund these payments, which is why it now says it must be free to sell as well as buy.

What is MSCI considering? MSCI has been reviewing whether companies whose main activity is accumulating digital assets, often called digital asset treasury companies, should stay in its global equity indices. It is assessing whether these firms are operating businesses or are closer to investment vehicles, which index providers often exclude.

Why does it matter? Exclusion could force index-tracking funds to sell Strategy shares, putting pressure on the stock and potentially on the company’s ability to raise money. It would also set a precedent for the growing number of similar companies. Saylor argues Strategy is an operating company comparable to banks and insurers, since it creates and sells credit products. He says the decision is not that important to the firm.

What happens next? MSCI is due to announce its decision on Friday, October 16. A decision to exclude would typically take effect at a later index review, giving funds time to adjust.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Singapore’s MAS holds policy steady, surprising all 10 analysts who expected tightening
item.description:
The decision is a dovish surprise against a unanimous call for tightening, which leaves the Singapore dollar vulnerable to some softening against its trading partners as positions built for a hawkish move unwind. The policy band still has an appreciating slope, though, so this is a pause in tightening, not an easing. Energy is the key swing factor. MAS explicitly flagged a sharp, sustained surge in energy prices as an upside risk, so a renewed jump in crude tied to Gulf escalation would put tightening firmly back on the table at the next review. Singapore’s position as a regional oil-trading and refining hub makes its imported inflation particularly sensitive to oil and refined product prices.

--

MAS chose patience over pre-emption, betting that slightly elevated inflation will ease on its own as the AI boom cools and import costs fade.

Summary:

  • The Monetary Authority of Singapore kept the rate of appreciation, width and centre of its S$NEER policy band unchanged
  • All 10 analysts polled by Reuters had expected MAS to tighten
  • MAS sees the economy expanding at a firm pace in the near term, then moderating as the AI cycle eases from its exceptional pace and global financial conditions tighten
  • Core inflation is forecast to average 1.5% to 2.0% in 2026, stay slightly elevated in the coming quarters and ease more discernibly from mid-2027
  • MAS said risks to inflation remain tilted to the upside, citing the potential for a sharp, sustained surge in energy or food prices

The Monetary Authority of Singapore kept its monetary policy settings unchanged on Wednesday, defying expectations for a tightening as it judged that slightly elevated inflation should ease over time.

The central bank, which manages policy through the exchange rate, said it would maintain the current rate of appreciation of its policy band, known as the Singapore dollar nominal effective exchange rate or S$NEER. There will be no change to the width of the band or the level at which it is centred. The band is already on an appreciating path, which helps restrain imported inflation, so the decision leaves that tightening bias in place without adding to it. All 10 analysts polled by Reuters had expected MAS to tighten.

MAS said the economy should continue to expand at a firm pace in the immediate quarters ahead, but moderate thereafter as the AI cycle eases from its exceptional pace and global financial conditions tighten. It expects AI-related activity to slow in the second half of 2027 and the economy’s positive output gap, a sign that demand is running ahead of capacity, to narrow through next year. The government will announce its growth forecasts for 2026 and 2027 in November.

On prices, MAS expects firming imported cost pressures to keep both core and headline inflation at their current slightly elevated levels in the months ahead. Core inflation is forecast to average 1.5% to 2.0% for 2026 as a whole, before easing more discernibly from the middle of next year as import costs ebb.

The central bank stressed that significant uncertainty surrounds the outlook and that, for now, risks to inflation remain tilted to the upside. A sharp and sustained surge in global energy or food prices could lift Singapore’s import costs by more than forecast. On the other hand, a larger-than-expected rise in interest rates or a sharper pullback in AI-related investment could drag on growth and, in turn, inflation.

The hold suggests MAS is prepared to look through near-term price pressures on the view that they will fade, while keeping its appreciating policy stance in place. With risks still skewed to the upside, the path of energy prices and the strength of the AI cycle are likely to shape whether it moves at its next review.

The Monetary Authority of Singapore is the coutnry's central bank.

item.title: Goldman’s Wilson picks two trades: US megacap tech and German fiscal winners
item.description:
The positioning data is the standout for traders. With hedge fund net exposure near the bottom of its multi-year range, a benign CPI print (preview) or a breakthrough in the Iran conflict could force investors back into stocks quickly, amplifying any rally. In Europe, the strong inverse link between equities and Bund yields means an energy-driven inflation scare would hit stocks and bonds together, so gas storage heading into winter matters as much as the oil price for European equities. The French-German bond spread is set to remain a barometer of euro-area political risk into next year’s presidential election, with the potential to weigh on the euro and French banks. Oil and gas remain the key swing factors for whether Europe’s discount narrows.

---

Goldman’s Wilson sees investors who have cut risk to the bone facing a market where earnings are still growing fast and valuations have already come down.

Summary:

  • Mark Wilson, head of European equities franchise sales and hedge fund coverage at Goldman Sachs, favours long US megacap tech and a basket of German fiscal spending beneficiaries
  • He said Europe is more vulnerable than the US to the energy shock, with European stocks and 10-year Bund yields more negatively correlated than at any time since the 1990s
  • Hedge fund net equity exposure has been cut to multi-year lows in response to higher rates and other uncertainties
  • Wilson sees US third-quarter earnings growth of around 27%, likely the peak, with Europe growing around 22% in the second half, or 15% excluding energy
  • Clients are focused on the French-German bond yield spread and European gas inventories heading into winter
  • He is watching US CPI, a possible break in the Iran conflict before the US midterms, and third-quarter earnings

Goldman Sachs’ Mark Wilson favours US megacap technology stocks and German companies set to benefit from fiscal spending, arguing that strong earnings growth and lower valuations leave a constructive setup despite higher bond yields and energy prices.

Wilson, head of European equities franchise sales and hedge fund coverage at Goldman Sachs, said in an interview published by the bank that Europe is more vulnerable than the US to the energy shock, given greater inflationary pressure. On a six-month basis, European stocks and 10-year German Bund yields are around minus 70% correlated, a degree of inverse correlation not seen since the 1990s, which he described as a regime shift. Natural gas is as much of a concern as oil for Europe, he said, and clients are closely watching gas inventories as winter approaches.

Clients are also focused on France, where the spread between French and German government bond yields has widened sharply over political tensions around the budget. Wilson expects the issue to remain a feature of markets in the months ahead of the French presidential election in the first half of next year.

Higher rates have driven a logical de-rating of equities on both sides of the Atlantic, Wilson said, with rate-sensitive sectors such as European renewables down by more than 20%. Investors have cut risk sharply. Net exposure among US fundamental long-short hedge funds sits near the bottom of its one-year range and in the lowest few percent of its three- and five-year ranges, while global funds are in the bottom tenth of their ranges.

Wilson rejected the view that Europe is a value trap. He acknowledged that higher energy costs are a real competitive headwind showing up in company numbers, but said Europe already trades at a discount, partly reflecting that, and has kept pace with the US this year. He pointed to investment themes in rearmament, energy independence and industrials, and said AI deployment could ease the drag from Europe’s demographics. European banks, he noted, have outperformed the largest US tech stocks over one, three and four years.

On earnings, Wilson expects US third-quarter growth of around 27% (UBS is at 28%), probably the peak for this cycle, while Goldman forecasts European earnings growth of about 22% in the second half, or 15% excluding energy companies. Although growth is slowing at the margin, he said high nominal growth combined with compressed valuations keeps the setup favourable.

His first trade is long US megacap tech. He argued that hyperscaler revenue growth lags heavy capital spending by several quarters and that returns on that spending are beginning to come through. His second is long German fiscal spending beneficiaries. German manufacturing surveys are outpacing the US, earnings estimates for the group have risen by around 13% to 14% this year, yet the stocks have de-rated by more than 20% and trade on low-teens multiples.

Looking ahead, Wilson flagged US CPI as key to whether yields can stop rising. He also sees a window for a break in the Iran conflict ahead of the US midterm elections, with third-quarter earnings set to shape views on the AI trade.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: UBS sees 28% Q3 S&P 500 earnings growth, says AI and cyclicals can lift US stocks
item.description:
UBS’s call gives investors a reason to look past this week’s chip-led selling. With semiconductors expected to deliver around half of index earnings growth, results from chipmakers and hyperscalers are the main test of the bullish view. The bank’s sector read favours industrials and AI-linked names over freight-heavy retailers and travel stocks, where energy costs bite hardest. Oil is the key risk. A further spike tied to Gulf escalation would widen the margin squeeze for goods sellers and test UBS’s view that the hit to overall profits stays limited. Today’s US CPI report is the near-term hurdle, since a hot core reading would push yields higher and weigh on richly valued tech.

---

Earlier:

  • US CPI preview: 14 investment bank forecasters see energy lifting headline to 3.6%, core held near 0.2%

---

UBS argues the AI boom and a sturdy economy can carry US profits, and stocks, through high oil prices and rising yields.

Summary:

  • UBS forecasts S&P 500 earnings per share growth of around 28% for the third quarter, supported by AI demand, firmer cyclical sectors and resilient consumer spending
  • AI-related spending is estimated to rise more than 80% this year to around $900 billion, and UBS expects semiconductors to account for about half of S&P 500 earnings growth in the quarter
  • Hyperscaler cloud revenue is seen growing close to 60% year on year, up from just under 50% in the June quarter
  • Higher energy costs are a headwind for freight-exposed retailers, goods makers and travel firms, but UBS sees a limited hit to overall profits
  • UBS says refinancing risk is manageable despite a rise of more than one percentage point in the 10-year Treasury yield this year

UBS expects a strong third-quarter earnings season to give US equities room to climb, arguing that artificial intelligence spending, healthy cyclical demand and resilient consumers outweigh the drag from high energy prices.

The bank forecasts earnings per share growth of around 28% for S&P 500 companies in the September quarter. Its view comes after a cautious start to the week, when technology shares led US stocks lower and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell almost 3% as investors waited for inflation data and earnings, with elevated oil prices and geopolitical conflict also weighing on sentiment.

AI remains the main driver of profits, according to UBS. It estimates AI-related spending will rise by more than 80% this year to around $900 billion and expects semiconductor companies alone to deliver about half of S&P 500 earnings growth in the quarter. Although capital spending growth is forecast to slow next year, UBS said the investment appears to be paying off for the large cloud providers known as hyperscalers. It expects their cloud revenue to grow by close to 60% year on year in the quarter, accelerating from just under 50% in the June quarter, with consumer AI agents seen as the next source of demand.

UBS also expects profit growth to broaden beyond technology. The new orders component of the ISM manufacturing index has stayed in expansion for nine straight months, and the bank noted that such stretches have historically lasted about three years on average. That suggests further room for growth among manufacturers and sectors such as industrials.

Consumers should hold up, in UBS’s view. Higher energy costs may squeeze spending at the lower end, but with initial jobless claims near multi-decade lows, the bank expects labour market strength to prevent a meaningful slowdown in overall spending.

UBS acknowledged that higher energy prices are a headwind, particularly for retailers and goods manufacturers exposed to freight costs. Travel-related companies are already feeling the impact, and manufacturers may face higher input prices. However, the bank sees only a limited effect on aggregate index profits.

Rising borrowing costs are also manageable, according to UBS. The 10-year Treasury yield has climbed by more than one percentage point this year, but non-financial S&P 500 companies have a weighted average debt maturity of about 11 years, meaning little of their debt is resetting to higher rates. UBS expects volatility to persist but sees scope for US stocks to move higher on the back of still-strong profit growth.

item.title: US CPI preview: 14 investment bank forecasters see energy lifting headline to 3.6%, core held near 0.2%
item.description:
The headline jump is largely priced in, so the market reaction will hinge on core. A print at the top of the forecast range, around 0.24% or higher, would back the Fed officials warning that inflation is broadening and firm December hike pricing, lifting front-end yields and the dollar. A reading at the soft end, near 0.16% to 0.18%, would support New York Fed President Williams’ view that price pressures are shock-driven and could trim expectations for tightening beyond this year. For oil, the report is a reminder that crude is now feeding straight into US inflation through gasoline. Any renewed spike in prices from Gulf escalation would show up in next month’s headline and keep energy at the centre of the Fed debate.

---

Earlier:

  • US CPI: Energy prices expected to lift headline inflation. Will core stay contained?
  • US CPI preview: energy set to lift inflation to 3.7%, core seen steady at 2.4%
  • MUFG: US CPI seen at 3.6%, core must surprise to revive an October Fed hike

---

Gasoline will do the heavy lifting in today’s US headline inflation, but the Fed’s next move depends on whether core stays as calm as Wall Street expects.

Summary:

  • US CPI for September is due Wednesday at 1230 GMT (0830 US Eastern)
  • The median forecast from 14 forecasters, compiled by The Wall Street Journal, sees headline CPI up around 0.6% m/m and 3.6% y/y, from 0.4% and 3.4% in August
  • Core is seen rising 0.22% m/m, down from 0.29%, with annual core at 2.4%
  • Core forecasts range from 0.16% at Deutsche Bank to 0.24% at Goldman Sachs, Barclays and Morgan Stanley
  • Forecasters are split almost evenly on whether annual core holds at 2.4% or edges up to 2.5%
  • The Fed’s Beige Book follows later on Wednesday, ahead of the October 27-28 policy meeting

US consumer prices are expected to post a sharp energy-driven rise in September, while underlying inflation is forecast to cool, according to a survey of Wall Street forecasters compiled by The Wall Street Journal ahead of Wednesday’s release at 1230 GMT (0830 US Eastern).

The median forecast across 14 forecasters points to a rise of around 0.6% in headline CPI for the month, up from 0.4% in August, lifting the annual rate to 3.6% from 3.4%. Core prices, which exclude food and energy, are seen rising 0.22%, slower than August’s 0.29%, leaving the annual core rate at 2.4%.

The headline boost reflects gasoline. US pump prices averaged above $4.30 a gallon in September, a record for the month, as the war involving Iran keeps crude prices high. Headline forecasts are tightly grouped, with Morgan Stanley at the top on a monthly basis and JPMorgan slightly below the pack.

The core picture is less settled. Deutsche Bank has the softest call at 0.16%, with Citigroup and JPMorgan both at 0.18%, while Goldman Sachs, Barclays and Morgan Stanley sit at 0.24%. The difference matters for the annual rate: roughly half of forecasters, including Bank of America, Goldman Sachs, Barclays and Morgan Stanley, expect core to edge up to 2.5% year on year, while the rest, including Citigroup, Deutsche Bank and JPMorgan, see it holding at 2.4%.

Part of the expected cooling reflects a one-off. Barclays and Morgan Stanley have noted that an unusual jump in wireless phone service prices lifted August’s core reading by around 0.1 percentage point and should partly unwind.

The release lands as Fed officials debate whether inflation is broadening. On Tuesday, Richmond Fed President Tom Barkin said inflation is proving enduring, and Boston Fed President Susan Collins said she is watching how widespread price pressures are. New York Fed President John Williams argued the economy is not overheating. A firm core print would strengthen the first camp. A soft one would support Williams’ view that the pressure stems from specific shocks.

There is also a measurement wrinkle. Core CPI has recently been running below core PCE, the Fed’s preferred gauge, which stood near 3% in August, so a benign core CPI print may flatter the measure the Fed actually targets.

The Fed’s Beige Book follows later on Wednesday, ahead of the October 27-28 policy meeting, where markets currently expect the central bank to hold before a December hike.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: How to read a whale alert: an Ethereum case study and a 5-point checklist
item.description:
How to read an on-chain whale alert before you react: an Ethereum case study

Early this week, an on-chain tracker reported that two wallets “linked to the Ethereum Foundation” had deposited 4,393 Ether (ETH), about $11.1 million, into the Kraken exchange. The post asked whether the Foundation was “dumping ETH again”.

  • Early Ethereum Foundation ETH recipients move $11M to Kraken: what the data shows

ETH fell 3.6% the following day, which seemed to support that reading. A day later it had recovered almost all of the loss.

Alerts like this one appear daily, and markets can react to them quickly. A few simple checks show how much an alert actually tells you. Here are five of them, applied to this week’s example.

1. Understand what trackers can see, and what they can’t

Every transfer on a public blockchain such as Ethereum is visible: which address sent coins, which address received them, how many, and when. Analytics platforms such as Arkham Intelligence and services such as Lookonchain turn that data into readable alerts.

Trackers can’t see who owns an address unless it has been identified, and they can’t see what happens inside an exchange. Once coins reach an exchange deposit address, any sale happens on the exchange’s internal order book, which is not recorded on the blockchain.

In this case: the blockchain confirms that the coins reached Kraken. It does not show whether they were sold.

2. Check the label: “linked to” can mean several steps away

Analytics firms attach labels to addresses, such as “Ethereum Foundation” or “Kraken Deposit”, using public disclosures, transaction patterns and investigation. A labelled address is useful, but a wallet described as “linked to” an entity may only have received coins from it at some point.

In this case: Arkham’s records show the Foundation sent 59,751 ETH to an intermediary address about a decade ago, when ETH traded near $0.90. That address later split the coins into three equal parcels of about 18,000 ETH and sent them to separate wallets. One of those wallets made the largest deposit this week. None of the downstream wallets carries a Foundation label. They are two steps removed from the Foundation. A former employee selling shares is not the same as the company selling, and the same logic applies here.

3. Know what an exchange deposit means

People usually move coins to an exchange so they have the option to sell, which is why traders watch exchange inflows. But a deposit is a preparation step, not a completed sale. The coins could also be used as collateral, moved between accounts or simply held.

Small “test” transfers often appear just before and after a large one. Senders use them to check an address before moving size, so they don’t reveal intent either way.

In this case: the main wallet sent 0.01 ETH, then about 2,998 ETH, then 0.004 ETH. That is standard practice.

4. Check the scale

Compare the size of the flow with the market it lands in. ETH regularly trades billions of dollars a day across major venues, so $11 million is a small amount. Even if all of it were sold, it would be unlikely to move the price much on its own. Holdings that haven’t moved yet can matter more than the flow itself.

In this case: based on the transfers visible on Arkham, the main wallet may still hold around 11,000 ETH from its original parcel, and the other two parcels from the same split may hold more. That remaining supply is the more useful thing to monitor.

5. Check the wallet’s history

A wallet that has never moved its coins and suddenly sends them to an exchange tells a different story from one that does so regularly.

In this case: the main wallet has done this before. About five years ago it sent roughly 4,000 ETH to Kraken in batches of 1,000 and 2,000 ETH. The pattern looks like an early holder taking profits in stages, not a new decision by the Foundation.

What the price did next, and why it proves little

ETH was trading near $2,535 when the deposits were made. It closed the next day at about $2,444, down 3.6%, then fell as low as $2,407 before recovering to around $2,507. That is roughly 1% below where it started.

The dip fit the alarming story, and the recovery contradicted it. Neither proves much. The bigger move came earlier: ETH fell about 8% between 6 and 8 October, before the deposits were reported. Tuesday’s low also matched the 8 October low almost exactly. That points to a market testing a level it had already found, not one reacting to $11 million of possible supply. A price move that follows an alert is not evidence that the alert caused it.

The checklist

Before reacting to a whale alert, ask:

  • Who controls the wallet? Is the label confirmed, or only “linked”?
  • What actually happened? A transfer, a deposit or a confirmed sale?
  • How big is it? Compare it with daily trading volume and with what the wallet still holds.
  • Is it new behaviour? Check the wallet’s previous activity.
  • What did the market already know? Was price already moving before the alert?

What to watch next

The wallets in this example still matter. If the remaining coins from the 18,000 ETH parcels start moving to exchanges, especially while ETH tests support near $2,400, the selling story would become more credible. If Arkham or the Foundation linked these addresses to the Foundation itself, the story would change materially. If the flows stop here, it remains a one-off move by an early holder, worth knowing about but not worth trading on.

The practical point is that a whale alert tells you to check the evidence before you react, not to act straight away. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: ICYMI - Three Fed officials signal inflation fight continues; Williams sees no 2027 hike
item.description:
With October largely priced out, Tuesday’s trio keeps December in focus for the next move. Williams’ comments on 2027 cap how far markets can push expectations for the peak rate. That should limit the upside for longer-dated Treasury yields and the dollar unless the data turns. Barkin’s warning that shocks are continuing gives the hawkish camp an opening if inflation stays sticky. Oil is the swing factor. Williams’ benign outlook assumes energy won’t add to inflation next year, so a renewed crude surge, for example from escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi energy sites, would undercut that view and strengthen the case for more tightening. For now, oil is effectively a direct input into Fed pricing.

--- Three Fed voices agree the inflation fight isn’t over; the open question is whether today’s shocks fade on their own or keep the Fed hiking into 2027.

Summary:

  • Richmond Fed President Tom Barkin said 2% inflation is achievable, that inflation is proving enduring and that it makes sense for the Fed to act, adding that AI investment is affecting inflation
  • New York Fed President John Williams said one more hike may still be appropriate in 2026, but he currently sees no reason for further increases in 2027
  • Williams expects inflation near 2% for 2027 as a whole and said the economy is not overheating, blaming energy prices and tech investment for near-term pressure
  • Boston Fed President Susan Collins expects a further hike before year-end and sees energy costs keeping inflation above target in coming months
  • Collins (two itmes, here and here, both hawkish!) said economic uncertainty is elevated and she is watching how broad-based inflation pressures are
  • The Fed raised rates to 3.75%-4.00% in September; the next meeting is October 27-28

Three Federal Reserve officials on Tuesday signalled that the fight against inflation is not over, with two backing one more interest rate increase this year, though New York Fed President John Williams suggested the tightening cycle may end there.

Richmond Fed President Tom Barkin, speaking at Howard University, said the Fed’s 2% inflation target is not out of reach and can be achieved. He said it is clear that inflation is proving enduring and that shocks to prices are continuing, making it sensible for the Fed to act. Barkin, who does not vote on policy this year, also said policymakers can see the effect of artificial intelligence investment on US inflation.

Williams, who is vice chair of the Fed’s rate-setting committee, told Bloomberg News he had not changed his view that one more rate hike may be appropriate in 2026. He said he currently sees no reason to believe the Fed would need to do more in 2027, though the outlook could change and policymakers must keep watching the data. Williams expects inflation to fall substantially next year to near 2% for 2027 as a whole, as tariff effects fade completely and energy prices stop adding to inflation. He acknowledged that high energy prices tied to the Middle East war and tech-related investment are lifting near-term pressures, but argued the economy is not overheating.

Boston Fed President Susan Collins struck a firmer tone. In prepared remarks, [she said she expects the Fed to raise rates a bit further before the end of the year] and described the risk of high inflation as elevated and the central bank’s main focus. She expects headline and core inflation to run above target in coming months because of higher prices for diesel, jet fuel and heating oil. In [follow-up comments, Collins said economic uncertainty is elevated] and that she is watching how broad-based inflation pressures are.

Together, the comments point to a Fed that agrees on the near-term direction but is split on the nature of the problem. Williams sees inflation driven by specific shocks that should fade, while Barkin’s emphasis on continuing shocks and Collins’ focus on the breadth of price pressures point to a risk that inflation proves more persistent.

The Fed raised its policy rate by a quarter point to 3.75%-4.00% in September. Williams’ comments late that month led markets to largely price out a hike at the October 27-28 meeting, leaving December as the more likely timing for the next move.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Goldman sees upside risks (105 EUR!) to its 70 euro TTF gas forecast as Europe stocks run low
item.description:
Europe’s gas market is now tied directly to the same Gulf disruption that is driving crude, so escalation in the Middle East lifts both energy risk premia together. If Europe has to outbid other regions for LNG this winter, the strain falls hardest on price-sensitive importers in Asia and emerging markets, tightening the global market further. Higher gas prices also feed through to European power costs and industrial margins, adding to inflation pressure. The upside skew also strengthens the economic case for burning oil products instead of gas where switching is possible, a modest extra support for diesel and fuel oil demand.

---

Goldman’s base case still sees European gas easing to 70 euros, but low storage and shrinking Mideast LNG flows mean the risks point the other way.

Summary:

  • Goldman Sachs says risks to its year-end TTF forecast of 70 euros per megawatt hour are skewed to the upside
  • Low European inventories and a month-on-month drop in Middle East LNG exports have supported TTF in the mid-80s
  • In a low-supply scenario with average weather, the bank estimates winter TTF would need to peak near 105 euros/MWh to cut enough LNG demand outside Europe
  • Goldman says uncertainty over winter weather widens the range of possible price outcomes further

Goldman Sachs sees the risks to its year-end forecast for European natural gas prices tilted to the upside, as low storage levels and falling Middle East LNG exports leave the region exposed heading into winter.

The bank’s forecast is for the Dutch TTF benchmark to stand at 70 euros per megawatt hour at the end of the year. That sits well below current levels, with Goldman noting that low inventories and a sequential drop in Middle East LNG exports have supported prices in the mid-80s. The gap implies the bank still expects some easing in its base case, but sees the balance of risks leaning towards higher prices.

At the centre of Goldman’s analysis is the question of how high prices would need to go to keep Europe supplied. In a scenario combining low supply with average winter weather, the bank estimates TTF would have to rally to a peak of around 105 euros/MWh. At that level, enough LNG demand elsewhere in the world would be priced out to free up cargoes for Europe. In practice, Europe would need to outbid other buyers, mainly in Asia, for a limited pool of seaborne gas.

Weather adds another layer of uncertainty. Goldman said uncertainty over winter conditions widens the range of possible outcomes further. A cold winter would accelerate storage withdrawals and intensify competition for cargoes, while a mild one would ease pressure on both inventories and prices.

The drop in Middle East LNG exports links the European gas market directly to the conflict in the region, which has already disrupted crude flows and shipping. Goldman’s assessment suggests gas traders will be watching Gulf export volumes and weather forecasts closely. With storage starting from a low base, Europe has less room to absorb either a supply shock or a cold snap than in a typical year, and the path of TTF this winter is likely to depend on how both develop.

Explainer: Understanding European gas pricing

TTF (Title Transfer Facility) The Dutch virtual trading hub for natural gas. TTF futures are Europe’s main benchmark for wholesale gas prices, much as Brent is for crude oil. When analysts quote “European gas prices,” they usually mean the front-month TTF contract.

EUR/MWh (euros per megawatt hour) The unit TTF is priced in. A megawatt hour measures the energy content of the gas, not its volume, so the price reflects the energy delivered. As a rough guide, a move from 70 to 85 euros/MWh is an increase of a little over 20% in the wholesale cost of that energy.

LNG (liquefied natural gas) Natural gas cooled to a liquid so it can be shipped by tanker. Europe relies heavily on LNG imports, which means it competes with buyers worldwide, particularly in Asia, for the same cargoes.

Demand destruction The point at which prices rise high enough that some buyers cut back or switch fuels. Goldman’s 105 euro estimate is the level at which enough buyers outside Europe would step back to leave sufficient LNG for European needs.

Injection and withdrawal seasons Europe typically injects gas into storage in the warmer months and draws it down over winter. Inventory levels going into winter are a key gauge of how well supplied the region is.

Sequential drop A decline compared with the previous period, here month-on-month, rather than year-on-year.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: investingLive Americas FX news wrap 13 Oct: Dollar retreats as traders await CPI; oil rises and stocks slip
item.description:
Tomorrow’s U.S. CPI report is the next big test for the markets. Will inflation remain concentrated in energy, or will the data show price pressures spreading more broadly? That question took on added importance after Susan Collins, president of the Boston Fed, reiterated her support for another rate hike before year-end.

Tuesday’s market moves were mixed. The dollar gave back ground against all the major currencies, longer-term Treasury yields moved lower, and stocks were modestly lower after a volatile session. Oil continued higher as Middle East tensions kept supply and shipping risks in focus. Existing-home sales beat expectations, but the report had little market impact.

Dollar gives back some ground

The dollar was lower across the major currencies in the late-session snapshot. Its largest decline was against the Canadian dollar, while its smallest decline was against the yen.

The currency levels showed:

  • EURUSD: 1.1196, +0.39%.

  • NZDUSD: 0.5611, +0.45%.

Higher oil provided a supportive backdrop for the Canadian dollar as did technicals (see post here).. More broadly, the dollar’s retreat reversed some of Monday’s strength as traders positioned ahead of CPI.

Longer-term Treasury yields ease

The late-session Treasury snapshot showed a modest rise in the 2-year yield, while longer maturities moved lower:

  • 2-year: 4.7974%, +0.64 basis points.

  • 5-year: 5.0085%, −1.25 basis points.

  • 10-year: 5.2168%, −2.72 basis points.

  • 30-year: 5.5660%, −3.33 basis points.

The curve flattened as longer-term yields fell more than short-term yields. The move offered some relief from elevated borrowing costs, but with the 10-year still above 5.2%, yields remain an important consideration for equities.

Stocks lower after a volatile session

The modest late-session declines hide a much wider trading range, particularly for the Dow. It was up 466.06 points at its high and down about 263 points at its low. The S&P and Nasdaq Composite also traded on both sides of unchanged. The Nasdaq 100 remained lower throughout the session.

The supplied late-session levels showed:

  • Dow industrial average: 51,675.16, −181.02 points or −0.35%.

  • S&P 500: 7,805.45, −1.79 points or −0.02%.

  • Nasdaq Composite: 27,204.38, −41.52 points or −0.15%.

  • Russell 2000: 2,783.37, −11.11 points or −0.40%.

  • Nasdaq 100: 30,569.48, −95.22 points or −0.31%.

Earnings begin, but buyers remain cautious

Earnings season got underway with reports from JPMorgan Chase, Citigroup, Wells Fargo, Goldman Sachs, Johnson & Johnson and UnitedHealth. In the earlier update, all six shares were trading lower.

The reactions underline that beating estimates alone does not guarantee a higher share price. Goldman Sachs beat both earnings and revenue expectations, while JPMorgan missed both. Traders also have to weigh guidance, valuations and the broader backdrop of higher energy costs and elevated interest rates.

European shares close mostly lower

European markets finished with small declines in most major indices, while Italy edged higher:

  • Germany’s DAX: 25,259.91, −0.07%.

  • France’s CAC 40: 7,827.64, −0.07%.

  • UK’s FTSE 100: 10,650.34, −0.06%.

  • Spain’s IBEX 35: 19,210.70, −0.39%.

  • Italy’s FTSE MIB: 50,057.17, +0.04%.

Collins focuses on the breadth of inflation

Susan Collins, president of the Boston Fed, said economic uncertainty is elevated and that she is watching how widespread inflation pressures become.

Her comments followed earlier remarks supporting another rate increase before the end of 2026. She highlighted AI and data-centre investment, tariffs and energy costs tied to the Middle East war as potential sources of persistent inflation.

For traders, the distinction matters. Higher gasoline prices can lift headline inflation directly. A broader rise in goods and services prices would suggest the pressure is becoming more entrenched—and give the Fed a stronger reason to tighten further. Collins’ comments kept that question front and centre ahead of CPI.

New York Fed President John Williams also spoke today and said one more rate hike is appropriate this year, but he currently sees no need for another increase in 2027. He expects inflation to slow considerably and approach the Fed’s 2% target next year, noting limited broader price pressures outside AI and energy and no signs that the labor market is fueling inflation.

The comments eased concerns about further tightening next year, helping push Treasury yields lower and extending the dollar’s losses. However, Williams did not signal rate cuts. His outlook remains dependent on inflation slowing as expected.

Home sales beat, but have little impact

September existing-home sales came in at an annualized rate of 3.99 million, above the 3.95 million estimate. Sales increased 1.5% month over month but remained 2.2% below a year earlier.

The South and West recorded monthly gains, the Midwest was unchanged, and the Northeast declined. Sales were lower year over year in all four regions.

Higher inventory and longer selling times are giving buyers more negotiating power, but rising mortgage rates remain a hurdle. The report offered a modest improvement in a still-soft housing market and did little to shift attention away from inflation and the Fed.

Oil rises as Middle East risks persist

Crude oil futures settled at $94.14, up $0.40 or 0.43%. The later supplied snapshot showed the CL1! contract trading at $94.93, up $1.19 or 1.27%.

Reports of discussions between President Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu about renewed action against Iran, threats to shipping near the Strait of Hormuz, and Saudi-led strikes against a Houthi-linked oil facility in Yemen kept escalation risks in focus.

The concern extends beyond oil supply. Sustained strength in fuel prices can raise transportation and production costs, keeping the broader inflation question alive.

Gold and silver fail to benefit from the weaker dollar

Spot gold was trading near $4,159.65, down $12.00 or 0.29%. Silver fell $1.164 to $59.1325, a decline of 1.93%.

A weaker dollar and lower longer-term yields would normally help gold. Tuesday’s decline shows those supportive moves were not enough to bring buyers in ahead of CPI. Silver’s larger fall also stood out, although the supplied data do not identify a specific catalyst.

Bitcoin rebounds

Bitcoin was trading at $83,314, up $1,568 or 1.92%.

The gain contrasted with softer equities and precious metals. The weaker dollar provided a supportive backdrop, but one session does not establish a lasting change in Bitcoin’s relationship with other risk assets.

CPI is the next shove

Wednesday’s September CPI report is due at 8:30 AM ET. InvestingLive’s preview points to headline inflation rising 0.6% month over month and about 3.7% year over year, with core inflation increasing around 0.2% monthly and holding near 2.4% annually.

The core reading and the breadth of price increases will be key. A firmer underlying number could revive expectations for an earlier Fed hike, while a softer reading would give policymakers more room to wait. Alongside CPI, traders will be watching oil, Middle East headlines and the next round of earnings.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Morgan Stanley lifts Brent forecast to $105 as costly freight favours short-haul crude
item.description:
The freight argument points to Brent holding a firmer premium over long-haul grades, including WTI delivered into Europe, for as long as shipping stays expensive. Refiners in Northwest Europe benefit from cheaper delivered barrels from Brazil, West Africa and the US, while producers of those grades absorb the cost through weaker differentials. The main risk to the call is a sustained fall in freight rates, for example from a durable normalisation of Hormuz traffic, which would remove the Brent-specific support even if overall supply stays tight. Traders should watch tanker rates and physical differentials as closely as the flat price.

---

Earlier:

  • Catch up time! Oil settles mixed, Brent near $106; booms reported near Aramco HQ in Dhahran

---

Morgan Stanley says Brent’s $100-plus price is no longer only about missing barrels: the cost of shipping them is doing much of the work.

Summary:

  • Morgan Stanley raised its Brent forecast to $105 a barrel for 4Q26 from $100, and to $100 for 1Q27 from $95
  • The bank notes Persian Gulf crude exports are back within 10% of prewar levels, yet Brent remains above $100
  • It says supply, inventories and geopolitical risk all matter, but Brent gains specifically from being a short-haul crude while freight is unusually costly
  • Long-haul grades from Brazil, West Africa and US WTI shipped to Northwest Europe have seen their prices fall against Brent to partly absorb higher shipping costs
  • The move follows an August upgrade that lifted the 4Q26 forecast to $100 from $75, citing a slow Middle East supply recovery and falling inventories

Morgan Stanley has raised its Brent crude forecasts for a second time in less than two months, arguing that unusually expensive freight is giving the North Sea benchmark a specific advantage over competing crudes.

The bank now expects Brent to average $105 a barrel in the fourth quarter of 2026, up from $100, and $100 in the first quarter of 2027, up from $95. Its analysts note that Persian Gulf crude exports have recovered to within 10% of their prewar levels, yet Brent continues to trade above $100.

Morgan Stanley said supply, inventories and geopolitical risk all play a part in keeping prices high, but one factor works in Brent’s favour in particular. Brent is a short-haul crude, delivered mainly over short distances into European markets, at a time when shipping costs are well above normal. Long-haul alternatives have had to adjust instead. The bank said crudes from Brazil and West Africa, along with US West Texas Intermediate, shipped into Northwest Europe have seen their free-on-board prices fall relative to Brent as sellers partly absorb the higher cost of freight.

The latest revision builds on a sharp upgrade in late August, when the bank lifted its Brent forecasts from a flat $75 assumption to $90 for the third quarter of 2026, $100 for the fourth quarter, $95 for the first quarter of 2027 and $90 for the second quarter. At that stage, Morgan Stanley pointed to a slower than expected recovery in Middle East supply stretching well into 2027, a market in deficit through the turn of the year, and steep declines in both oil-on-water and onshore inventories, including in China. It also flagged a record gap between crude and refined products, with gasoil trading far above Brent.

The new note shifts the emphasis. With Gulf exports now largely restored, the bank’s case leans less on missing barrels and more on the cost and logistics of moving oil, a dynamic that particularly benefits Brent.

The outlook still depends heavily on how the Middle East conflict develops. Freight costs and shipping security through the Gulf are now central to whether Brent can hold above $100 into next year. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Catch up time! Oil settles mixed, Brent near $106; booms reported near Aramco HQ in Dhahran
item.description:
The deferred curve is carrying the bigger signal. WTI for calendar 2027 hit a record for a 12th straight session, around $84, and Brent’s 2027 strip set records on Monday near $90. That suggests the market is pricing a lasting supply deficit, not just a front-month war premium. Diesel remains the pressure point, with product strength outpacing crude and keeping refining margins elevated. With the Dhahran reports coming late in the day, the Asian open is the first real test of how much Aramco infrastructure risk gets priced back into Brent. A narrower Brent-WTI spread also points to Middle East risk being offset at the margin by the prospect of more Russian barrels.

---

I'm doing a bit of a catch up on crude if its of any use to anyone. 

Earlier:

  • Crude oil futures settle up $0.40 at $94.14

---

Oil is caught between a Russian diesel deal that promises more supply and a Saudi-Houthi war that now reaches the doorstep of Aramco’s headquarters.

Summary:

  • Brent settled down nearly $1, or circa 1%, at around $106, after Monday’s highest close since mid-September; WTI rose about 40 cents to around $94, its highest close since late September
  • Hopes the US-Russia diesel export deal could free up Russian supply offset Middle East risk; the Kremlin said the deal has no direct link to Ukraine peace talks
  • Loud booms were reported near Saudi Aramco’s Dhahran headquarters amid an escalating Saudi-Houthi war; Aramco did not comment
  • OPEC said OPEC+ output rose sharply in September, led by Saudi Arabia lifting crude production to around 8.4 million bpd from around 6.2 million in August
  • OPEC cut its 2026 demand growth forecast for a sixth straight month and raised next year’s outlook, citing the need to rebuild inventories depleted by the Iran war
  • Trump accused the Houthis of trying to drive up oil prices before the US midterm elections

Oil prices settled mixed on Tuesday as hopes that a US-Russia deal on diesel exports could release more supply from Moscow offset an escalating conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis that threatens Gulf energy infrastructure.

Brent crude futures settled at around $106 a barrel, down nearly $1 or circa 1%, after closing on Monday at their highest level since mid-September. US West Texas Intermediate rose about 40 cents to settle at around $94, its strongest close since late September, Reuters reported.

The Kremlin said it saw no direct link between the diesel deal and its position on Ukraine peace talks. It was responding to a Reuters report that US President Donald Trump’s envoys had told Ukrainian officials the arrangement was part of an effort to bring Russia back to negotiations. Trump said the Russian diesel was destined for the rest of the world rather than the United States. US diesel futures still traded up circa 5%, a sign the market remains unconvinced the deal will ease tight product supply. Diesel prices have recently hit record highs in many regions after Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy sites and Iranian attacks on Middle East infrastructure.

In the Gulf, loud booms were heard on Tuesday night near Saudi Aramco’s headquarters in Dhahran, the centre of the kingdom’s oil industry, according to six sources cited by Reuters. One source said the building had been struck, though it was unclear whether by a direct hit or falling debris, and an evacuation order was issued, four sources said. Aramco did not comment. The Saudi-led coalition said fragments of an intercepted missile had fallen on a residential area.

Earlier, the coalition had targeted a Yemen Petroleum Company fuel depot on the outskirts of Sanaa, according to Houthi-run media, and the Houthis threatened Saudi oil facilities in response. The group has spent a week firing missiles and drones at Saudi targets, including Riyadh’s international airport. Trump accused the Houthis of deliberately trying to push up oil prices ahead of the US midterm elections and said he would make a decision on Iran very soon. Separately, reports said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had discussed with Trump last week the possibility of a joint operation against Iranian military and nuclear targets, a call that came before Trump said he would not strike Iran ahead of the midterms. Iranian authorities said a tanker they described as violating rules caught fire in the eastern Strait of Hormuz.

item.title: Fed’s Collins says uncertainty is elevated as she watches breadth of inflation pressures
item.description:
Collins’ focus on how widespread inflation is moves attention to core and services prices, not just the headline energy-driven numbers. Signs of fuel costs spreading into broader prices would firm December hike pricing and support front-end yields and the dollar. For oil, that means sustained strength in crude and products now carries a second-round risk the Fed is explicitly watching. Her stress on elevated uncertainty also leaves room for the data to delay the next move, which caps how aggressively markets can price an October hike.

---

Collins has already called for another hike, and now she is spelling out what will set the timing: whether inflation spreads beyond energy in an uncertain economy.

Summary:

  • Boston Fed President Susan Collins said economic uncertainty is elevated
  • She is watching how broad inflation pressures are in the incoming data
  • Collins said she is very focused on inflation data and looks at the economy as a whole when considering rate policy
  • The comments follow her earlier remarks backing a further rate rise before the end of 2026
  • The Fed lifted its policy rate to 3.75%-4.00% in September, and several officials have pointed to December over October for the next move

Boston Federal Reserve President Susan Collins said on Tuesday that economic uncertainty is elevated and that she is paying close attention to how broad-based inflation pressures are, as she set out the factors that will shape her view on the timing of the next rate move.

Collins said she is very focused on the inflation data and that she looks at the economy holistically when weighing the future path of policy. Her emphasis on breadth suggests she will be watching whether price pressures spread into a wider range of goods and services, rather than staying concentrated in a few categories.

The comments add detail to remarks earlier in the day in which [Collins said she expects the Fed to raise rates again before the end of 2026]. In that speech text, prepared for a banking conference at the Boston Fed, she said she had supported the central bank’s quarter-point hike in September, which took the policy rate to a range of 3.75% to 4.00%, and called the risk of high inflation the Fed’s main focus.

Collins has flagged several forces that could keep inflation above the Fed’s 2% target, including investment in data centres and artificial intelligence infrastructure, the ongoing effect of tariffs, and energy costs linked to the war in the Middle East. She has said she expects both headline and core inflation to run above target in coming months, citing recent increases in prices for refined fuels such as diesel, jet fuel and heating oil.

Her baseline outlook remains constructive, with healthy growth, a job market near full employment and a gradual return of inflation to target. Her latest comments make clear, however, that she sees the outlook as uncertain and that the incoming data will decide how quickly she wants policy to move.

Policymaker projections released in September pointed to one more increase this year. Several Fed officials have suggested in recent weeks that it is more likely in December than at the October 27-28 meeting, and Collins has said the policy path into the new year will depend on the data.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
