item.title: Economic and event calendar in Asia Wednesday, October 14, 2026 - China inflation data
item.description:
China releases consumer and producer price data for September at 0130 GMT on Wednesday, which is 9:30 pm US Eastern time on Tuesday. Factory-gate inflation is the reading most likely to move markets, as higher global energy costs continue to feed through the economy.

August sets the benchmark. Consumer prices rose 0.8% y/y, up from 0.5% and in line with forecasts, while the 0.4% monthly gain beat expectations. Producer prices climbed 3.8% y/y from 3.5%, with the statistics bureau pointing to rising energy prices.

There are three things to watch.

  • The first is producer prices. The August increase reflected imported inflation, with higher crude oil and non-ferrous metal prices lifting petrochemical and smelting prices at home. Another firm print would confirm that the oil shock is still working its way through Chinese input costs.
  • The second is pass-through to consumers. Headline CPI remains well short of Beijing’s informal target of around 3%. Analysts warn that a weak property sector and soft consumption make it hard for downstream manufacturers to pass on higher costs, and that factory prices could slip back towards deflation once supply-side support fades. A widening gap between strong PPI and modest CPI would point to a squeeze on margins, not demand-led inflation.
  • The third is core CPI, which excludes food and energy. It gives the clearest read on whether domestic demand is firming or whether energy is doing all the work.

Trade figures for September are also on the calendar. In August, exports rose 18.6% y/y and imports 21.7% in yuan terms, with import growth outpacing exports for a sixth straight month. The dollar-denominated surplus was around $119 billion.

For markets, a hot PPI would add to signs that China is passing higher goods prices on to the rest of the world after years of exporting disinflation. A soft CPI would keep the focus on weak household demand and support the case for further policy easing.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Fed’s Collins backs another rate hike by year-end, flags three inflation pressures
item.description:
Collins’ remarks reinforce expectations of another quarter-point rise before year-end, with recent Fed commentary leaning towards December rather than this month’s meeting. That should keep front-end Treasury yields supported and limit room for a sustained dollar pullback while hikes stay in play. For oil traders, the significance is the feedback loop: further gains in crude and refined products tied to the Middle East war now feed straight into Fed hike expectations, so energy strength carries rates and dollar consequences. A softer run of data would be the main thing to cool that pricing.

---

Earlier:

  • Fed Williams: Sees no need for rate hike in 2027 at this time

---

Collins sees a resilient economy as giving the Fed licence to keep tightening, with war-driven fuel costs the clearest reason inflation won’t get back to target on its own.

Summary:

  • Boston Fed President Susan Collins expects a further rate increase to be appropriate before the end of 2026
  • She supported last month’s quarter-point hike that took the policy rate to 3.75%-4.00%
  • Collins called the risk of high inflation elevated and the Fed’s main focus, with inflation above target for more than five years
  • Her baseline sees healthy growth, a broadly balanced job market near full employment and a gradual return of inflation to 2%
  • She flagged data-centre and AI investment, tariffs and Middle East war-driven energy costs as risks, expecting headline and core inflation above target in coming months
  • Timing of the next move depends on data; several officials have signalled December rather than the October 27-28 meeting

Boston Federal Reserve President Susan Collins said on Tuesday she expects the US central bank will need to lift interest rates again before the end of 2026, arguing that further tightening is needed to return inflation to the Fed’s 2% target in a timely and lasting way.

In prepared remarks for a banking conference at the Boston Fed, reported by Reuters, Collins said she had supported the Federal Open Market Committee’s decision last month to raise its policy rate by a quarter of a percentage point to a range of 3.75% to 4.00%. She indicated that a modest additional increase would likely be appropriate this year, while stressing that her view on both the need for and timing of further action would rest on the full body of incoming data and how it shapes the balance of risks.

Collins framed the inflation fight as the Fed’s central task. With growth holding up and the labour market broadly balanced, she said policymakers have room to concentrate on bringing inflation back to target, a goal the Fed has now missed for more than five years. She described the risk of persistently high inflation as elevated and the central bank’s main focus at present.

Her baseline outlook was largely constructive. In what she called the most likely scenario, the economy keeps growing at a healthy pace, the job market stays close to full employment and inflation eases gradually back to 2%, helped by ongoing efficiency gains that keep supply and demand in balance. She added that a stable labour market should continue to underpin consumer spending.

Collins nonetheless identified three forces that could complicate that path: heavy investment in data centres and other artificial intelligence infrastructure, the continuing effect of tariffs, and higher energy costs linked to the war in the Middle East. She said she expects both headline and core inflation to run above target again in the coming months, pointing to the recent jump in prices for refined products such as jet fuel, diesel and heating oil.

Projections published at the September meeting already pencilled in another increase before year-end. Several Fed officials have signalled in recent weeks that the move is more likely to come in December than at the October 27-28 meeting, and Collins’ comments keep a further hike firmly on the table while leaving its timing open. She said the policy path into the new year would depend on the data.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: US CPI: Energy prices expected to lift headline inflation. Will core stay contained?
item.description:
The US CPI report for September will be released tomorrow at 8:30 AM ET. The report - along with the PPI on Thursday - will give traders another key piece of the inflation puzzle as markets assess whether the Fed will need to tighten policy further. Number crunchers will also be able to get a handle on the PCE and Core PCE from both readings. 

The expectations are seeing: 

  • Headline CPI month over month: +0.6% expected versus +0.4% last month.

  • Headline CPI year over year: +3.6% expected versus +3.4% last month.

  • Core CPI month over month: +0.2% expected versus +0.3% last month.

  • Core CPI year over year: +2.5% expected versus +2.4% last month.

The core numbers will be the focus.  A 0.1% MoM (or better) core and 2.4% (or better) YoY would be moving in the right direction. . 

The key question: How far are energy costs spreading?

Higher energy prices are expected to drive the stronger headline reading.

The more important question for the broader inflation outlook is whether those costs are filtering into other goods and services. That puts the core reading—which excludes food and energy—firmly in focus.

Last month, gasoline prices rose 3.9%, accounting for more than one-third of the monthly headline increase. However, core prices also rose 0.3%, with increases in categories including airline fares, lodging and used vehicles. Traders will be watching whether those underlying pressures ease in September.

A 0.2% monthly core reading would represent a slowdown from August, even if the annual rate edges higher. Those two measures can move in different directions because the annual comparison also depends on the reading from a year ago.

What could it mean for markets?

My read is that the core surprise will be an important driver of the reaction:

  • Hotter core inflation: A reading of 0.3% or higher could lift Treasury yields and support the dollar as traders reassess the risk of further Fed tightening. I am leaning that a October hike - although it may be needed - is odds on a no go for political purposes. The Fed will let the market do the tightening for them and remain out of the hot seat (it is just the way it is with Trump as President).  

  • Core in line at 0.2%: That could give the Fed more room to wait, particularly if the headline increase is concentrated in energy.

  • Softer core inflation: A reading of 0.1% or lower could pressure yields and the dollar and provide some relief for stocks. Although December may still be on the table (one more hike), the chance for October works closer toward 0% from about 20% currently.  

For currency traders, the data will provide the shove. The technical levels will help tell us whether buyers or sellers can keep control after that initial move.

Watch where the price trades relative to the pre-release range, nearby swing levels and the 100- and 200-hour moving averages. A break that holds carries more weight. A break that quickly reverses tells us the market had its shot—and could not follow through.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: USDCAD sellers regain control, but key swing support stands in the way
item.description:
The USDCAD extended to a new high for the year on Friday following the weaker-than-expected Canadian jobs report. However, the breakout could only stretch about 7 pips above the previous yearly high near 1.4292 before reversing lower.

The buyers had their shot. They could not keep the break going.

By Friday’s close, the price had rotated lower. Selling continued on Monday until the pair reached its rising 100- and 200-hour moving averages—the blue and green lines on the chart. Buyers leaned against those levels and pushed the price higher.

That rebound stalled near Monday’s closing level and below the previous yearly high at 1.4292. Today, sellers have taken back control, pushing the pair lower in a more trend-like move. The USDCAD is down about 0.48%, making the Canadian dollar the strongest performer against the US dollar.

Sellers reach the next downside hurdle

The decline has reached the top of a swing area between 1.41922 and 1.4204. That area is defined by swing highs and lows going back to September 29, highlighted by the red numbered circles on the chart.

So far, the price has stalled near the upper boundary at 1.4204.

Sellers have secured a victory with the move below the hourly moving averages. To increase their control, however, they need to break below this swing area and stay below it. That would open the door for further downside momentum toward the next swing area between 1.41297 and 1.4153.

Can buyers defend support again?

If buyers hold this area for a fourth consecutive test, the focus shifts toward a rebound to the 100- and 200-hour moving averages near 1.4250.

Those moving averages become the next upside hurdle. Getting above—and staying above—them would weaken the sellers’ control and bring the yearly high near 1.4298 back into focus.

For now, sellers are enjoying the victory today, but they still have work to do. The 1.41922–1.4204 swing area is where their next test begins.

The trading lesson

A break below the moving averages shifts the short-term bias, but the next support area still matters. Sellers need to see follow-through. Buyers need to see support hold.

Use the swing area to define risk and judge control. Hold support, and buyers have a reason to lean against it. Break below and stay below, and sellers earn another victory.
